blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're due to start with the evidence shortly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I would just be grateful if I could raise one matter just to state our position on one part of the arrangements that arises.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It has been brought to our attention that the two prosecution experts, certainly Dr Bohin, and as I understand it, Dr Evans, are keen to be in court, in this court, during proceedings from this point.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That comes principally as a request from Dr Bohin after giving evidence. Up until this point they've been in the alternative courtroom, which of course has provided acceptable facilities.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I recognise it's certainly not a matter for the defence, in the absence of any very specific reason, to seek to say who should or shouldn't be in court, so we don't put it as high as that. We simply observe at this point, with our view of the case, that it isn't the optimal arrangement that we would -from our view.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's something that we do not find attractive. We know it isn't our decision, but it's important I say this given what we have seen and what we anticipate.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We do not regard it as attractive and we question how appropriate it is in a case where they are in the position they are in and will return multiple times to give evidence. However, it's a matter for the court.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's not something we can object to any more firmly than that, but we raise our unhappiness and concerns with that arrangement.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, yes. Conventionally, of course, experts sit behind counsel.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But that can't be done at this stage. The original arrangements were, given this was a small court, that family members of those involved in this case would be accommodated in the courtroom and they are. Family members, children, one side, and the defendant the other. I'll hear what Mr Johnson says.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can state my position: it's all or nothing, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I made that absolutely clear. I spoke --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All or none.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- to Mr Worthington -- after I had sent the message, I spoke to him face-to-face and made it clear that was the position: unless all could be accommodated I accepted that none could be accommodated. One can't have preferential
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: treatment for one side or the other, so there's no dispute about that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No -- sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I should just say, our concern wasn't all or one in the sense that we know Dr Hall is quite content with the arrangements in the other court, he's able to work there, listen to the evidence and probably is the more comfortable. So we don't anticipate we would seek to bring him into court and we don't raise any question because of any apparent imbalance in that; that's his choice. It's just in the circumstances of this case, we question the need for it and why it happens. But as I've made plain, my Lord, at this stage it's not anything that we will take further than that, but we do identify our concerns and it's an area we haven't finished with yet.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson, why is it particularly desired? Because if I was in that situation I would rather have a desk where I could put my laptop on and take notes or write or whatever it is rather than sitting in a chair that --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think the perception is that it's better to see things in the flesh than via a screen. I think it's as simple as that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, they see everything that we see and hear everything that we hear. Let's not spend time on it now. For the moment I am not going to accommodate this request. One factor is that the jury sit there and they sit there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And they may not, consciously or subconsciously, react to any piece of evidence, but it just adds a risk that doesn't need to be added.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Understood.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Also, there may be other -- that may fill up there --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Oh, undoubtedly it will from time to time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 7.38 on the 14th, Lucy Letby messages Jennifer Jones-Key saying:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Sorry if I was off. Just wasn't a great start to shift but sadly it got worse x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies at 8.42:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "You weren't off, you just weren't happy and there's nothing I could say that was going to make it any better. To be fair, didn't have the energy neither.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: I'm wiped after them 2 days. I don't mean you but sometimes I don't think people realise how hard it is in 4 with all the babies and parents, et cetera. My mind gone lol. Hope you're feeling slightly better and get some sleep x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. That's 8.42. The next message from Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 8.48 she replies with:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "I was struggling to accept what happened to [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Now we've lost [Baby C] overnight and it's all a bit much x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: At 8.53 Jennifer Jones-Key replies:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It will be but it does happen to these babies, unfortunately. Maybe [you'll] feel better when you know what happened to [Baby A]. Was [Baby C] in 1? I'm all confused. It's a very sad part of our job and I think cause we don't see it as much it's harder. We lost a baby in N4 and I beat myself up over it but it was
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: overwhelming sepsis and nothing would have saved they (sic) baby."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 8.57:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "[Baby C] is the little 800g baby. Went off very suddenly. Sophie was looking after him. I know it happens but it's still so sad and cruel isn't it x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies at 09.00:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Yeah, was around when he delivered. Sophie helped [redacted] with him. It is and it's horrible and you have to be strong though as especially he's parents need you to be. blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 09.07:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Sophie devastated. She couldn't stay in the room during resus but did very well. [Nurse B] was fine actually but think it'll hit her once home. Parents didn't stay long. Caroline B cried when came on today. Jo been told by phone and upset. Yvonne has taken over paperwork etc today for him x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies at 09.11:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Glad she did okay. Don't mean this rudely, it might do [Nurse B] some good. Yeah, bet Jo gutted as he had a good day but they always do. This is where we have to pull together and look after each other. You need to try and switch off and get some sleep x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 9.13:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "We worked really well and Mel was great. Think we all supported each other brilliantly, just such a shock especially after Mon. [Nurse B] went out bright and breezy, only one who didn't cry, but think it was just an act. I'll try. Just leaving now x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies at 09.14:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Yeah, that's what you'll need. I think it was just a front from [Nurse B] and maybe she felt she had to as was in charge and not appropriate. Switch off for a bit."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key continues with another message at 09.15:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "I feel sorry for Yvonne to all the crap only ever happens when Eirian away and she won't appreciate how hard we've all worked this week [as read]."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 09.22:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It's been horrible for all involved and would be when Eirian away. Anyway, it's happened and have to carry on x"

blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "We lost a little one overnight. Very unexpected and sad xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Susan Letby replies at 09.27:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Ahh sorry to hear that xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies to Lucy Letby at 09.30:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It has been for you guys but does affect us guys too and the parents in 3 and 4. Okay x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies to Jennifer Jones-Key at 09.38:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It affects everyone xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies at 09.39:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Defo. Hoping you're going to be okay. This isn't like you, sending you biggest hugs xx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy replies to Susan Letby at 09.40:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "He only weighed 800g. Sophie, the new girl, was looking after him. She's devastated."

blocks.text: And there's a bit that's not relevant to this:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Hope you have a good day xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies to Jennifer Jones-Key at 09.41:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "I think it's harder to deal with here than at Women's. I just keep seeing them both. No one should have to see and do the things we do. It's heartbreaking but it's not about me. We learn to deal with it.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Susan Letby replies to Lucy Letby at 09.42:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Ah, so sad. Try and have a peeps. We are so proud of you. Love you xxx Just on our way x."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 09.43:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Love you xxx"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies to Lucy Letby at 09.43:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It is horrible and heartbreaking and I don't think them babies ever leave you. I remember mine. Course it's about you [too] but also about everybody. Northern term: chin up chuck and will get through it together."
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 09.45:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "It's not about me or anyone else. It's those poor parents who have to walk away without their baby. It's so unbelievably sad. Thanks, we will x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "When are you next in work?"

blocks.text: "Tuesday. You?"

blocks.text: "Damn. Infection? Crap week. How's [Baby B]?"

blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Damn. As quick as [Baby A]? Yeah, shit week [sad face emoji]."

blocks.text: Jennifer Jones-Key replies to Lucy Letby at 10.01:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "I know but it does still hurt. Hope [they're] going to be okay. Try and rest x"

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies to [Nurse A] at 10.05:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Yes, pretty much. Hey carried on with resus whilst waiting for dad and priest to arrive, by then had HR of about 30. Stopped but he carried on with HR and gasping for several hours. Horrible."

blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "That's so sad. Don't know want to say. Try and sleep xx."

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replies at 10.09:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "There are no words. It's been awful. I'll try x"
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: [Nurse A] replies at 10.12:
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: "Yes. A really tough week esp for you."

blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Surfactant, is that just a record of the fact that he had been provided with surfactant as part of your desire and designs from the previous day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, you can give multiple doses of surfactant as well, so it was a record of how many doses he'd needed.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: What about the lactate record here? It says 4.3, does it say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It does, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: What, if any, significance would you have attached to that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's a high level for the lactate. A high lactate in itself is a sign rather than a diagnosis and it needs to be reviewed in context of the whole baby and any other clinical signs. It also needs to be noted in context with what the trend of that lactate has been, which I haven't documented there, and whether that was increasing or decreasing.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So you say it's a sign rather than a diagnosis of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it's not a diagnosis of anything in itself. It's a sign that he -- multiple different conditions could cause your lactate to rise and it's a sign to look for those conditions.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving down a paragraph, we have the letter F -- for fluids, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: What have you recorded under that sub-heading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've documented that he's still on 90ml per kg per day and he's now getting TPN and he's having it via a UVC.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: I've documented that his blood sugars are stable, he's passing urine at 6.8ml per kg per hour, that he's not opened his bowels yet, and that the humidity had been reduced in the incubator yesterday but had now been increased again.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: What, if anything, do those readings inform you of when taken together and in addition to the respiratory data that you've recorded?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So all of those findings help you work out how much fluid you think the baby should be on at that time.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: It's -- all of those things are very stable signs that you would expect for a preterm baby. If his urine output -- depending on how high his urine output was, that might alter how much fluid you gave him, so documenting that is important.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. The next paragraph. S for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sepsis. So any infection concerns. Then I've just written that he was screened yesterday, so a septic screen, so since I left someone had started him on antibiotics, so he was on benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. The CRP that had been sent off -- I think that number is a 1 next to what I've written, which is a normal low level of CPR, and that a blood culture had been sent.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: In this context does "screened" just mean tested?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. So the day before you understand that the test had been taken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The fact that he was now on those antibiotics, does that demonstrate the results from the tests had been received and taken into account or not necessarily?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not necessarily. It would have been standard practice if we wanted to test for an infection to start antibiotics at the same time and wait for the results to come back rather than waiting for the results and then starting antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So is that a precautionary measure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So the CRP, what does that -- if it is a -- 1 and it's your handwriting, you think it is -- what does that inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's a low level of CRP or a normal level of CRP.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Anything less than 10 we would say is normal.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: What does CRP levels inform the doctor of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the CRP is a protein that goes up in infection. So it wasn't raised so didn't suggest that there were any signs from that blood test of an infection at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So taking those all in combination and together with everything else recorded on that page, under the heading "Sepsis", was there anything to suggest the onset of sepsis in [Baby C] at this stage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't know the exact reason the antibiotics were started, because that wasn't on my shift, so I don't know if the reason for starting the antibiotics indicated some level of infection, but the results that we have back and the fact he's having antibiotics could be sort of a standard practice for a baby of that gestation. But I didn't make the decision to start the antibiotics so I can't comment on the level of concern at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could scroll down, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next paragraph, M -- does that stand for metabolics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Metabolic concerns, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And the notes record that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've written "bili", which is for bilirubin, of 91.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: All bilirubin measurements, which is a sign of jaundice, are documented on a separate chart to indicate if treatment is needed or not and I have documented that it was just over the treatment line.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So a measure of 91 is just over the treatment line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For a baby of that gestation at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. And crossing the treatment line, as it were, in this context, does that necessarily thereafter trigger treatment?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It means that phototherapy treatment would be started, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. "CV" is cardiovascular?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And "no concerns" speaks for itself. The next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mean blood pressure of 36, which would be a normal mean blood pressure for a baby of his gestation.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: L?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For lines, so what access, what lines he had in. He still had a peripheral cannula and a UVC.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Meds?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The medications in total that he was on, so caffeine and the dose of 5mg per kilo, benzylpenicillin, gentamicin and nystatin.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Taking them inn turn. Caffeine, is that something particular to [Baby C] or is that medication that would be given to all such premature babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: All premature babies of his gestation would be started on caffeine.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. The other entries, are they a reiteration of the antibiotics that you've already described to us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and nystatin, which is a prophylactic treatment for fungal infections for preterm babies, so as prophylaxis rather than treatment.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Can you help us with what that means?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To prevent him getting a fungal infection rather than treating him for one.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: N for neurology?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, any neurological concerns. I have written that he handled well.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Why would you record that the fact that he handles well?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What's the significance of that to you, the clinician?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If a baby is very irritable or upset or distressed or if a baby's very quiet and not responding to any interaction, both of those would be worrying signs for a variety of different reasons.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. So not susceptible to being recorded as data, but important information to you, the clinician?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So next we have, do we, a list of observations?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So examination findings.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Is that OE or IE?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: O/E, so "on examination".
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Observations on examination.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you very much. We know he handles well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Next?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I've written that he was active and that he was pink, well perfused, and his capillary refill time is 2 seconds, which is a normal capillary refill time.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: I have then written his heart sounds of 1 plus 2 plus 0, which is a way of documenting normal heart sounds and no added sounds.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have written that his chest sounded clear but he still have some slightly increased work of breathing slash tachypnoea, which is an increased respiratory rate, but good air entry. That his femoral pulses are palpable, his hips were normal, his palate was normal, he had normal male genitalia, although the testes were not descended. I had not checked his eyes but for his spine I have written NAD, no abnormality detected.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. I won't go through them one by one, but the femoral pulse palpable, what's that indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's feeling for the pulses in his groin and checking that you can feel them. If you can't feel the pulses in the groin that is a sign that there might be something wrong with his circulation.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: In [Baby C]'s case it was palpable, so you could feel it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: That's that a sign of or an indicator of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's normal, that's what you'd expect.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. So putting them all together, those observations on examination, together with all the data that we've already been through, what was the general picture here in relation to [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That he was responding as any preterm baby of that gestation would and as to be expected at 30 weeks' gestation.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Hence you put in place, if I may say so, would this be a generic plan?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So nothing in particular designed to address any specific need or requirement that [Baby C] had been exhibiting as part of your examination of him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. These are all just fairly standard sort of next steps in the plan for caring for a preterm baby.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So the first next step is to take the blood gases in the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So we normally do them at different time frequencies, so specifying the next time I wanted one taken of 1 pm. Then I've documented an arterial line, which again can be very common in preterm babies. It helps measure the blood pressure and also take blood tests more directly from the line rather than having to use needles on the baby to take blood tests.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then I've put check U&Es and CRP. So urea and electrolytes, which is how his kidneys are functioning, and the salt levels in his blood. And the CRP, which is the infection level, to see if that had changed. We normally do these most
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: days for preterm babies and I have written that if the sodium is ever high, that we would need to increase the fluids because that would indicate he needed more fluids than he was currently on.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So that's not a reaction that you are making yet but you're putting a marker down just in case?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it's sort of pre-empting what might be seen on the tests.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So phototherapy because of the bilirubin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, phototherapy because the bilirubin was above the treatment line.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: A cranial ultrasound scan, so that's what the CRUSS stands for, which we would do on day 1 or day 2 for all preterm babies.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: To start trophic feeds, so a very small amount of feed, if available. Often this is not enough to quantify and give regularly, so trophic feeds is just to start a little bit.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Is that primarily to trigger the digestive system as opposed to provide nutrition to the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And then I've written to continue the CPAP because his blood gas is stable on that and to update the parents.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you go to 1916, please? Not your entries, entries from a colleague, Dr Beech. But does this record that as you had planned, the cranial ultrasound was undertaken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Another entry from a Dr Rylance, a fact that I think you were informed of later, that records -- thank you -that at 7 in the morning on 12 June 2015, and I'll just read it:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Reviewed. UVC found in bed."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that a fact that was shared with you at a later time, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall specifically being told or not being told.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Very well. Then we'll move on, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll go to tile number 77. Pausing there so we can orientate ourselves in terms of time. It's now 9.30 in the morning on Saturday, 13 June. Your next shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: We can see in the form that mirrors the notes from the previous shift that we've just been through, a summary is given here, but if we go beneath it, please, to see Dr Ogden's own notes. Again, are these your ward round notes, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. So [Baby C] born at a gestational age of 30 weeks and a day. Now he's in day 4 of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The problems are the special features that you recorded at the point of his birth. They still exist, they're his background --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: -- issues. And then do we see in the same format, your list of observations upon examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So again, V for ventilation. I won't ask you to go through each and every one of these. But in general terms, what do those recorded readings and data tell you? What did they tell you at the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He's in less oxygen than he was a few days ago and his blood gas is still a normal blood gas. The lactate has come down. He's on a different amount of fluids now but what's changed -- he was having these very dark, bilious aspirates. That describes the colour of any fluid that was coming out of his feeding tube.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: I'll come to that recording in the next paragraph.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Just in terms of the respiratory readings, as compared to yesterday's, as it were, what does that tell you in terms of [Baby C]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that suggests that his breathing is stable and possibly improved from a day or two before.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go to fluids. The first line just records what he's receiving?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Then you were telling us about the entry or the finding that is recorded on the next line. Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've documented that he had very dark bilious aspirates/black aspirates, and that these are aspirates that would have come up the feeding tube that he will have had in place. That will have been taken from the nursing records, what they aspirated from that tube.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. You probably answered this question, but spell it out. When you say they would have come up the tube, would that have been spontaneously or would they have been aspirated manually by the treating or caring nurse?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Potentially either. I haven't specified in my notes, but sometimes they can come up spontaneously, sometimes they need aspirating.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. You've made more than one reference here to the colour of the aspirates. Why and what does that inform you potentially of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So bilious or dark green coloured or black aspirates aren't normal colour for aspirates. They would suggest that there was potentially a concern with his abdomen and the way he was tolerating any feeds, if he'd been on them, or how his bowel was responding to being preterm.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The findings you have recorded in those terms, would they have been a concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that would have been a concern.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Concern because they might indicate what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: They may have indicated a condition called necrotising enterocolitis or potentially infection.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving through the other entries on the fluids paragraph, urine, then a measure of his output.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Anything exceptional about that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: "Bowels not yet opened." This is day 4 of life; anything significant about that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In itself not necessarily, but it would be taken in context with his aspirates, how his abdomen examined, how much feed he'd been having. By itself it's just a statement that they'd not been opened yet.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. "Not started feed yet" speaks for itself.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Those were -- his sodium result was 142 and his potassium was 3.4, both of which are within normal limits.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. You've noted to the side here -- is that a reference to an X-ray --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Abdominal X-ray, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: -- taken on 12 June? So that's the time of the X-ray -date of the X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Does it follow that you examined that X-ray, that picture?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It would suggest that I had seen the X-ray. All I've documented is what it showed, but I can't remember whether that was looking at the X-ray or reading someone's interpretation of the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So to assist the jury in that regard, an X-ray is taken either as part of protocol or in response to a specific request by a clinician such as you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Examined on the ward by the clinician?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at the time the X-ray was taken.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: At the time it was taken, and another doctor told, and then subsequently considered by a radiologist?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. S for sepsis, suspected sepsis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Is that based on any of the other findings on this page or is that for the same reasons as you've recorded the day before?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm unsure because I don't know exactly what happened between my two entries as to whether there were any other additional concerns, so it may be the same infection screen or it may have been a different one.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: I don't know from my notes if that was a new concern or not.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. You reiterate the antibiotics that he'd been prescribed and was receiving.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So he was on benzylpenicillin and gentamicin still.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Then we have the CRP, which on your last corresponding set of notes was at 1, if you were reading your handwriting correctly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: But now this appears to read "1, 23". What does that tell us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that shows us the repeat level of the CRP had gone up to 23, which is elevated and is higher than a normal range of CRP, so would suggest that there was some element of an infection that he had.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: I'll come back to that in a moment, but does it follow that at least your note-taking convention is to record each entry, "1, 23", and then --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It appears so, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So plainly, it's elevated as compared to the previous day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: But in more general terms, how high is a reading of 23?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we would treat a -- we would be worried. Any CRP higher than 10 would be suggestive of an infection, but the range that a CRP can increase to is very variable and can be up to 100 or higher. In itself, the number doesn't always signify the severity of an infection, it's just a marker that there's an infection there, that it's in that spectrum of above normal but not as high as it could potentially be.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: But nonetheless, one of the factors that would go into consideration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've written that his blood culture was negative, which shows that it hadn't grown any specific bacterial infections.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Let's take a step back. Blood would have been taken from [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at the time the antibiotics were started.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So we're now going back 24 to 36 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. From whenever that day/time was, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: But at this time when you're making these notes, does it follow that you have received information from the testing of that blood?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, we normally get interim reports from blood culture results anywhere from sort of 24 to 48 hours after the blood culture is taken. But at any time, if it were to grow an infection -- and a final result usually comes about 5 days later. But at this point in time the blood culture wasn't growing in infection.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Just to spell that out, colleagues elsewhere are monitoring the blood taken from [Baby C] to see whether there's any evidence of bugs, bacteria, I suppose; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was being analysed by the microbiology lab.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And at this point, the latest information was that it was negative, there were no such bacterial --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: -- developments within that blood. Is that, like the elevated CRP on the line above, is that another of the factors to be taken into consideration when assessing whether or not there was sepsis, NEC or what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it would be taken into account with everything else. You can have babies or patients that are unwell with an infection that have a negative blood culture and you can have
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: patients that have positive blood cultures for a variety of different reasons.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: On the next entry there's reference to "LP". You'll correct me if I'm wrong, I think might be lumbar puncture?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: You record that [Baby C] had not yet had a lumbar puncture?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And the reason for that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that his platelets were low. So you would want a relatively stable platelet count before doing any tests where there was a potential for any bleeding and a lumbar puncture has a potential to cause bleeding at the site.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: How did you know that his platelets were low? Is that contained within some of the other data in this document or from somewhere else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I haven't documented it in those notes there, but I would have seen his full blood count result on some other set of investigation results, which would have documented that.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Right. The low platelet count, as shown by the downwards arrow, as well as militating against undertaking a lumbar puncture, what, if anything else, of significance would you attach to that reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That could have been low from an infection, from necrotising enterocolitis or the background of having uterine growth restriction.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next, the cardiovascular entry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've written that his mean blood pressure is 36 to 40, which would be normal readings for his gestation, and that there was no cardiovascular concerns.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've documented the neurology that he handles well and that the cranial ultrasounds, I've written NAD, so no abnormality detected when it was undertaken on day 2.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you, the next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again for the metabolic concerns that he's now off the phototherapy yesterday and that the bilirubin level today is 111. That would need to be taken in context with the bilirubin chart.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. These are also your entries, it's a continuation of the data that you were just alluding to there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So this is where I've documented next the blood test results that we had back.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Does that tell you anything additional to that that you have already conveyed to the jury in the last few minutes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It just quantifies that platelet count that I mentioned was low, was 39.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. What does a reading of 39 tell you? Is it in the spectrum of a platelet count for a baby like [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's just a low platelet count. Normal would probably be above 150. The level of how low it is doesn't necessarily indicate anything.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So --
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: The lines generally, forgive me.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So L for lines. He now has a long line, which would be a peripherally inserted central line that was in through his left saphenous vein and he had a cannula in his right hand.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: And the saphenous vein?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a vein in the foot.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Does it run up the leg?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It does, yes.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: Thank you. So you are recording that one was in place but you didn't put it in place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I'm just documenting its presence.
blocks.speaker: OGDEN

blocks.text: So we often are reassured if the CRP doesn't go up or goes down, because if it goes down, that shows an improvement. blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is, yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Right. So he's been on phototherapy and it seemed to be working, is that a layman's --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think so, yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: And a positive sign of what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So your lactate can go up for a number of different reasons, including infection, dehydration. It kind of tells us how well your organs are being perfused and how well your tissues are being perfused with blood and with oxygen. So there's a number of reasons why it can go up.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: In short that measurement has it still on the high side but you would have been pleased to read that it was lower than the last corresponding measurement?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Thank you. I think that was the extent of your involvement with [Baby C] on that day, although you were back on on 12 June 2015 and if we go to -- there we are -- exhibit J1918. Same page, of course. Forgive me.

blocks.text: Further down the same page, you are noting that here, a long line was inserted?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: By you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: -- for the introduction? So the first attempt was through the right saphenous line?

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That means further up towards the middle of the body, so higher up than where the bruise was but in the same vein.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: So effectively you were steering around the bruise; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, avoiding it by going higher up, yes. And I have said that the same thing happened, the vein bruised and I couldn't get it past that bruise, so I took it out again.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Thank you. So they were two attempts on the right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: So the third attempt was on the left?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Same vein, different limb, obviously?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: And this was successful?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Long line threaded to 11 centimetres as measured"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Explain that to everybody, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. As is the protocol, did you cause an X-ray to be taken of the baby so you could satisfy yourself or inform yourself, more accurately, as to the position of the long line within the baby?

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: And then a dash or an arrow, "Happy" --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "With position".
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: So as well as causing an X-ray to be taken, you considered the X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: I think Mr Murphy, if we could go to J1996.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see there an X-ray that says it's timed at 12.36 on 12 June 2015. The notes we were just looking at were timed at 12.45. Obviously the notes have to be made after the event.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Thank you. So that's the X-ray that you considered and deemed the long line position to be satisfactory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: I'm not sure they were your words, but if we could go back to J1918, I won't misquote you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You were happy with the position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: Sorry. So having arrived at that, you then removed the — is that the guide wire?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: We heard a little about that. Is that something within the long line that helps the clinician steer it through?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's more to enable you to see it on an X-ray because the plastic tube of the long line wouldn't show up on an X-ray. Whereas the guide wire is a very thin piece of metal so you can see it. That's why you leave it in until you've X-rayed and then you can see it.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: So you X-rayed, you considered the X-ray, you were happy with it, then you removed the guide wire and you attached a device referred to as an octopus?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.text: And just could you tell us what that is?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a little device that goes on the end of a line, which enables the nursing staff mainly, whoever's giving medications through that line, to attach a syringe or an infusion and give it -- put it into the line, give the medications.
blocks.speaker: BEECH

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Deputy manager.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Deputy manager. What was your role back in 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, yes, I was the deputy manager in 2015.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: We've heard reference to various job titles amongst the nursing staff at Chester back in 2015. Back then, were you a band 5 or a band 6 nurse? Can you remember?

blocks.text: A band 6.

blocks.text: You were a band 6 nurse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've been asked to speak up -- oh, the witness.

blocks.text: Yes. I think your voice can be heard quite clearly.

blocks.text: A senior nurse practitioner is a band 6 nurse that's done extensive neonatal training. So you would do a foundation and your intensive care. blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Therefore, not all band 6 nurses would be senior nursing practitioners?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, and that's distinguished with the uniforms -it's a darker navy -- on duty.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Back in 2015, were you a senior nursing practitioner?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. You know that you've been invited here this afternoon to give evidence about the care that you provided to a baby on the unit by the name of [Baby C], who was on the unit in June 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: What we will do during the course of your evidence, Ms Griffiths, we'll take you to nursing notes and the like that were created at the time, so you're not going to be tested as to the precise detail of observations and the like and -- that's what the jury were referring to a few minutes ago -- you're going to see it on screen.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Before we look at your nursing notes, can you confirm for me, and I know this is not controversial, that you made notes during the day shift of 12 June 2015, but when you completed those notes, you effectively misfiled them, so the notes pertaining to [Baby C] temporarily went into the file relating to another, completely unrelated baby --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: -- whose name we don't need to share with the jury? And when you realised the error, you extracted them out of that file and later put them into the correct file?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So that was just a simple admin error that was soon corrected?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Let's go to those notes. So Mr Murphy, members of the jury, this is a note that will be in the side folder, not behind a tile, and it is exhibit reference J1950.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I want to focus, please, on the right side of the page. That set of entries there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's just deal with the admin error, which is dealt with on the first line there, "YG" being your initials, and you have described that admin error by:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On reflection, notes from the 12 June day shift were written in [ie they were filed in and we have blocked that baby's name out] for [Baby C]."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So [Baby C]'s notes were filed in another baby's file?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Then you extracted them. So the nursing notes were printed and rewritten. So from your original note you created this note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. So this note is, could you confirm, a narrative of what you observed on the day during the time that you were caring for [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. It says you assumed care of the infant at 20.00 hours; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 8 o'clock in the morning.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: That's an error. So it reads 8 o'clock at night, it should read 08.00 hours, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. You recorded that he, [Baby C], was receiving the assistance -- receiving assistance with ventilation throughout the day; yes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And that was nasal CPAP?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. And you recorded the pressures that were being applied and the level of oxygen and variations within that band. We've already heard evidence about that so we won't dwell on that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next line, could you help us with that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Nares red but not broken. DuoDERM applied."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. That's the nares. We are always concerned about the nose, the bridge of the nose, with the prongs, just to make sure that there's no rubbing with the prongs.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And is that a typo or was that a term you use, nares?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Nares, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: What does it mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The nares is just the bottom of the nose.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: The bottom of the nose. So there's some reddening --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: -- of the baby's skin, although the skin was not broken, is that what that means?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's right. It's just a little bit red so sometimes we alternate between a mask and prongs.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So you applied DuoDERM, which is some emollient, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DuoDERM is a little dressing that's just placed there and it prevents any sores or broken skin.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your narrative note records next that there were "No apnoeas noted", so no episodes of him stopping breathing during --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: -- during your observations of him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Caffeine was given as prescribed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: You have recorded, and we've already heard from Dr Beech, how a long line was inserted by Dr Beech?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Because the long line was now going to perform the role that the cannula had previously been put in place for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: "[Baby C] was unsettled at times."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you expand upon that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because [Baby C] was corrected at 30 weeks, he was quite lively, so he was -- I just remember vividly that he only loved to be held by parents in a kangaroo style.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So I think that's what we mean by being unsettled, he just liked to be held.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And that's what "kangaroo care" means in this context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: The long line or the position of the long line was Xrayed and, once Dr Beech was satisfied with it, the introduction of fluids into [Baby C] through the long line was commenced; is that what that note --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: -- tells us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then at 18.30, so getting towards the end of your shift, back end of your shift at least:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bile noted on blanket."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that an observation that you made, do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And do you recall that observation independently of this note or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Can you expand upon it in the circumstances then or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: With any baby, because obviously we're worried about introducing feeds too early because of the antenatal (inaudible) diastolic flow, so we would always be really cautious with any milk feeds that we were giving. And then we always would aspirate with the NG tube just to make sure there wasn't anything in the tummy, particularly air.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But on this occasion there was -- sometimes you can aspirate bile but -- I think it must have been noted on the bedding that there was a little bit of bile.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So the fact that you've observed and recorded "noted on blanket", does that tend to suggest that the bile had come out spontaneously as opposed to through aspiration by a nurse?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Then does it flow, because of that, the nurse, you I should say, aspirated the nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We would do that quite frequently anyway. With a baby being on nasal CPAP we would always aspirate the abdomen at least every few hours, 4 hours, but obviously with the bile that is an indicator that you would need to aspirate just to make sure.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Upon aspirating the NG tube, did that produce or withdraw 2ml of black-stained fluid?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's what's written, yes, that's what I've recorded.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And full stop. Separate note:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "The infant [that is to say [Baby C]] was too unsettled for lumbar puncture."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would that have been -- firstly, how unsettled he was, would that have been an observation you made or somebody else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Usually, if there's an indication -- if the CRP is rising, and I think in this instance it did, then we would
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: always do a lumbar puncture, but obviously we were quite mindful because it is a needle into the spine, so if the baby's too active or too upset then we wouldn't perform that because we wouldn't want to take the risk of him moving.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: That decision to defer or postpone the lumbar puncture, would that have been a decision made by you, made by one of the doctors or made together?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's always a joint decision.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. So it was deferred and the plan was to reassess that decision --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: -- later? And we know Dr Ogden considered the baby and advised, at the time, feed should be withheld to be reconsidered at a later stage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And that is your note. I think that is all of your notes in relation to that shift that ended at about 8 pm on 12 June. Can you remember who you handed over to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was Melanie Taylor.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether or not you had any further direct dealings with young [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I actually came into work on Sunday for an early -- a shift and that's unfortunately when [Baby C] had died, on the previous night, so I did help Mel with caring for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: That was at a time after his death?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. But in life, your cares provided to him in life, are they summarised in this paragraph that we've focused upon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you remain there and answer any further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

Ms Griffiths, [Baby C] was really just about at the limit of what you could accept at the Countess of Chester at this time, wasn't he; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We accepted under 27 weeks and 800 grams.

blocks.text: You'd said that he was a very small baby and we know that. He was intrauterine growth restricted and 800 grams and your view was you didn't often have babies of that weight for that gestation, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's right.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Normally, and you help us by giving a comparison, you'd normally expect at least 2 kilograms even for that gestation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So [Baby C] was very small. Is it right, if he'd just been about 10 grams less, he probably wouldn't have been able to stay at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But as a general rule, in an ideal world, 800 grams is the lowest limit, isn't it, for the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When they're born, yes.

blocks.text: When they're born.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: I think you explained to the police that things are very uncertain about the outcome?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think any admission on to the neonatal unit, it's very uncertain.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: You said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby C] was very small and very vulnerable and it was a very precarious time"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Things are very uncertain about the outcome of a baby that small; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Correct.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Marked distension of the stomach and the small intestine."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you know how that would happen whilst [Baby C] was in your care or on the shift that you were working?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I say, because we have nasal CPAP, sometimes air can be in the tummy so that's why we do aspirate. It can be a sign of infection, but I know he was covered on antibiotics, so I can't comment any further.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: What I wanted to ask was, if that's right, even if aspiration was taking place through the NGT, it's still possible, so far as you can see, for the stomach to distend like this with air going in through CPAP?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I suppose it all depends when I last aspirated the stomach as well with air.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So, to make it quite clear what we're discussing, aspirating a stomach involves drawing out the contents of the stomach through the tube that's going into it, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And that could involve drawing out fluid?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Or it might involve drawing out air if there's air in there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Is it right then you're saying [Baby C], so far as you recall, would have been aspirated over this period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We tend to aspirate every 2-3 hours because obviously you are not going to aspirate every hour, because then you are disturbing the baby. So we do tend to let the baby rest in the incubator.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But in your opinion the most likely explanation, notwithstanding aspiration, is this is air that has gone in through the CPAP that's giving him extra oxygen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Possibly.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Possibly. There could be other reasons?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to move forwards now to the notes you made. Page 1950. That's in the additional section, ladies and gentlemen, so you can scroll down there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just some questions about these, Ms Griffiths. If we could go to the right-hand side, please, and just enlarge the notes there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think we've explained that the notes had been entered at the right time but in a different place and then you brought them across to [Baby C]'s notes on 14 June; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Right. So that's how it is that we have an entry at 1738 on the 14th dealing with notes from the 12th?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. I just want to ask about one area in particular:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bile on the blanket and the aspirated black fluid."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Where bile on the blanket is concerned, that is most probably bile that's been brought up through vomiting; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Or dribble.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Or dribble?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But it's come back up through [Baby C] through his own body acting that way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. The 2ml of black-stained fluid, that's an aspiration that you or you and the doctor have taken?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would have taken that.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: You would have taken that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Thank you. Just pausing there, if we look in the clinical charts, and they're at page 2009, and there is an S on this, it's slide 39, or if you are using the J numbers, 2009.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We need to enlarge on the right-hand side, please, Mr Murphy. If we could make that a bit larger, and we might zoom in yet. I'm just going to -- after we've looked at what this is, I'm going to ask you to explain to us, Ms Griffiths, as best you can, where you think the aspiration you're talking about is.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is 12 June. With got the hours running down the left-hand side. We probably need to go to the bottom half of the form, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we can see -- it's a little difficult because we've got a big red J2009 right over the area perhaps where you might want to look. When you describe taking out the -- is it 2.5ml of bile?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Is it possible from what you can see there to tell us what entry that would be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually I would put it between the 18 and 19, but perhaps it's not there, but sometimes I would put it on the ITU chart or if I've written the notes at 7 o'clock then it would be fresh in my mind.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: All right. Can I check, where we look on the right-hand side, there is a column which looks like there is a Y (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But in any event, we're not disputing that you did do it, I was just seeing if we could see it on the chart.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was all. You can't identify it; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: All right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you agree, Ms Griffiths, that dark bile coming up is a matter for some concern with a baby like [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think any bile we're cautious with. The main thing we would do is just stop feeds, which -- we weren't feeding anyway.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But you certainly recognised it as a potential issue of some sort?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and I think, you know, we would -- that's why with lines in the tummy we're always very careful, but he didn't have a line in his stomach, so if we would have still had the UVC and that dark bile, we might have taken a line out, thinking --
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But that wasn't the case.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And is it the more serious if the baby has vomited bile up?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... It was just -- I mean, he didn't desat with the vomit, so I wouldn't say it was... you know, obviously it's not good, but it was more of a dribble on the actual bed that I noted. So it wasn't him, [Baby C], desatting that made me go over and then see that he was vomiting.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: But would you agree it's necessary, inevitably, to keep a close watch over a baby like [Baby C] in any event?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: And certainly if we're dealing with dark bile, whether it's aspirated by the doctors or the nurses or whether it's by vomit, that could be a matter of concern, so you need to keep a close look on him?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: So I'm not asking two questions at once, it is potentially -- potentially -- a serious issue, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think given that we're nil by mouth and he had bile, yes, I would -- and I think I did get the doctor to review [Baby C] at that time.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Yes, Dr Ogden, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you, Ms Griffiths.

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: aspirating from babies. Then we looked at, and could we please go to, a chart, the intensive care chart, which again is in the additional documents at J2009, and if we could highlight the right side of this document, please, as we did a short while ago.

blocks.text: The jury have been shown the like of this before.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: But just to remind ourselves, it's divided into two parts: input and output. There is a column under "output" -- let's read them. "Blood sugar". The next says "NG asp/vomit". Are you familiar with this?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: What's recorded in that column, "NG asp/vomit"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I haven't recorded anything.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: No, but what's that column for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is more when we're doing feeds because, obviously, if we're introducing feeds we want to make sure that that feed has been absorbed. So if we were going to give 10ml of milk then we would always aspirate the tube before we actually give that NG feed to make sure that that feed had been absorbed. But because [Baby C] wasn't receiving feeds then I didn't fill that column in, but normally we would just record feeds there or if we had bile, so we wouldn't necessarily record 10ml of air.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Are you able to measure the aspirated air or gas in the same way?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, you can aspirate and it can be 10ml and then you disconnect, and then it escapes, and then attach again, or sometimes you can put an NG tube on free drainage so that it's constantly releasing air.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Is there any record that we could go to to see, firstly, whether [Baby C]'s tube was on free drainage or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Unless it was written in the medical notes or in the nursing notes, I wouldn't be able to say.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Right. We may return to that. But just focusing still with this column "NG asp/vomit", I don't want to misquote you, but did you say a moment or two ago that you may not have necessarily recorded if gaseous aspirates were drawn?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: As a matter of record, if we scroll down to when your entries again at 08.00 hours on this chart, we can see -- I'm looking at the initials YG.
